introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education (GCE) Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Philosophy 2 (0790), Paper 2 (Philosophical Culture), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Duration: three hours.**

Candidates are expected to answer FOUR (04) questions chosen from the three sections imperatively (that is, with questions taken from each of the three sections).

Each essay must contain:
- An introduction = 5 marks
- A thesis = 7 marks
- An antithesis = 6 marks
- A synthesis = 3 marks
- A conclusion = 4 marks

Each question carries 25 marks.

Candidates are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation of material.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : la page de garde dit « answer FOUR (04) questions chosen from the three sections imperatively » (quatre questions au total, prises dans les trois sections). Le sujet ne dit pas explicitement « au moins une par section » ; cela est déduit de « imperatively » et du format des autres années. `regles_choix` porte le minimum, une règle `parmi 1 sur 2` par section (Section One : questions 1-2 ; Section Two : questions 3-4 ; Section Three : questions 5-6) ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`. Les deux sous-sections de la Section Three (Descartes, texte de philosophie africaine) sont comptées comme une seule section de deux questions ; le sujet ne dit pas si un candidat peut traiter les questions 5 et 6 à la fois.

Points : chaque question est imprimée « 25 marks » (4 x 25 = 100). Les critères de la page de garde (introduction 5, thèse 7, antithèse 6, synthèse 3, conclusion 4 = 25) s'appliquent aux dissertations (questions 1 à 4) ; les questions de textes (5 et 6) ont leurs propres points par sous-question.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les auteurs et positions cités (Sophistes, Socrate, Kierkegaard, Nkrumah, Nyerere, Gyekye, Wiredu, Mbiti, Césaire, Fanon, Descartes, Hume, Kant...) sont ceux de l'histoire de la philosophie établie, sans citation littérale ni numéro de page ; les dates et faits historiques cités sont donnés dans leurs grandes lignes. À faire relire par un enseignant de philosophie avant mise en avant.

Sujet scanné (3 pages) avec filigrane gcerevision.com et bandeau publicitaire sans incidence sur la lecture ; aucune figure. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Philosophy 2, Paper 2 (Philosophical Culture), code 0790, JUNE 2021, trois heures.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Colonialism is synonymous to the dehumanisation of the African. Do you agree?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction (5 marks).** Colonialism is the domination of one people by another through conquest, occupation and control of land, labour and government; in Africa it followed the Berlin Conference of 1884-85. To dehumanise a person is to deny his or her full humanity: to treat him as a thing, an animal or an inferior being. "Synonymous" means that the two words have the same meaning, so that colonialism and dehumanisation are one and the same. The problem is whether colonialism, by its nature, always meant dehumanising the African, or whether it was only one source of dehumanisation among others, and whether it had other aspects.

**Thesis: I agree that colonialism was fundamentally dehumanising (7 marks).**

*Racial ideology.* To justify conquest, European thinkers spread the idea of a hierarchy of races. Hegel, in his lectures on the philosophy of history, described Africa as outside history, and Lévy-Bruhl presented a "primitive mentality" of the colonised. Such theories treated the African as a child or a savage who had to be led; colonial domination presupposed this inferiority.

*Practices.* Forced labour, compulsory porterage, the hut tax, the seizure of land and the brutal regime of the Congo Free State, and the indigenous legal status which gave the African fewer rights than the colonist, treated people as tools of production. The earlier transatlantic slave trade had already made human beings into goods, and colonialism inherited that mentality.

*Philosophical testimony.* Aime Cesaire, in Discourse on Colonialism, writes that colonisation produces "thingification": the colonised becomes a thing. Frantz Fanon, in The Wretched of the Earth and Black Skin, White Masks, shows that colonial rule rests on violence and creates in the colonised a feeling of inferiority and a divided self. Albert Memmi describes the colonised person as deprived of his own history and initiative. Steve Biko and the negritude movement of Senghor and Cesaire react against this denial of African personality. Cultural alienation (the devaluation of African languages, religions and customs, and the teaching of European history as the only history) was another form of dehumanisation, which Ngugi wa Thiong'o later called colonisation of the mind.

**Antithesis: the two are not synonymous (6 marks).**

First, dehumanisation of Africans is older than colonialism (slavery and slave trade, including trade run by African as well as Arab and European traders) and has outlived it: some post-colonial regimes have oppressed their own peoples, and racism and poverty persist. Colonialism is therefore not the only cause, and ending it did not end dehumanisation. Second, the concepts are not identical in meaning: colonialism is a political and economic system, dehumanisation a moral attitude and treatment. It is possible to define the first without the second. Third, colonialism had other effects, some of which Africans themselves used: schools and mission education that trained many of the leaders of independence, new written languages, medical services, roads and railways. Colonial authorities and missionaries were not all the same: some individuals defended African rights. These benefits do not excuse the system, since they were mostly designed to serve colonial interests, and many were paid for by African labour, but they show that colonial life was not simply and only dehumanisation. Fourth, Africans were not passive: they resisted, adapted, and used colonial institutions to claim their own humanity.

**Synthesis (3 marks).** Colonialism was not synonymous with dehumanisation in the strict sense, because the two terms do not mean the same thing, and dehumanisation has other causes. But the logic of colonial domination depended on denying equal humanity to the African, so dehumanisation was essential to it, not accidental. The answer is that colonialism was inseparable from dehumanisation, without being its only cause.

**Conclusion (4 marks).** I therefore agree in substance, with a qualification. Colonialism, built on racial hierarchy, forced labour and cultural denial, was in its very structure a dehumanisation of the African, as Cesaire and Fanon argue. But it is wrong to identify the two completely: there were earlier and later forms of dehumanisation, and colonisation also had effects that Africans used. The task that follows from this is rehumanisation: political independence, restoration of African cultural dignity and a new humanism, which Fanon himself called for.
